title: The Photovoltaic Effect
description: How light becomes electricity — from Becquerel to silicon

concepts.title: A Brief History
concepts.contentHtml:
The photovoltaic (PV) effect — generating an electric voltage from light — was first observed by Edmond Becquerel in 1839, aged just 19, using silver-coated electrodes in an electrolyte.

The mechanism stayed mysterious until Einstein's 1905 paper on the photoelectric effect (which won him the Nobel Prize, not relativity) explained that light comes in quanta — photons — and a single photon either has enough energy to release an electron or it does not. Wave intensity is irrelevant.

Modern photovoltaics began at Bell Labs in 1954, when Chapin, Fuller, and Pearson built the first practical silicon solar cell with ~6 % efficiency. Within four years, Vanguard 1 carried PV cells into orbit — and the satellite industry has powered itself with them ever since.

concepts.title: Photons and Band Gaps
concepts.contentHtml:
A semiconductor has a forbidden energy range — the band gap E_g — between its filled valence band and empty conduction band. Three things can happen when a photon strikes the material:

  • Photon energy below E_g → photon passes straight through (transmitted, wasted).
  • Photon energy equal to E_g → an electron is lifted from valence to conduction band, creating an electron-hole pair. Most of the photon's energy is captured.
  • Photon energy above E_g → an electron-hole pair is created, but the excess energy is rapidly lost as heat (thermalisation) — the electron drops to the band edge.

For silicon, E_g ≈ 1.12 eV, corresponding to a wavelength of about 1100 nm (near infrared). Photons longer than that are invisible to a silicon cell.

concepts.title: Why Silicon?
concepts.contentHtml:
Of every photovoltaic material studied, silicon dominates real-world deployment — over 95 % of installed PV capacity. Why?

  • Its band gap (1.12 eV) is reasonably close to the optimum for the solar spectrum (~1.34 eV).
  • It is the second most abundant element in the crust — supply is essentially unlimited.
  • The microelectronics industry already perfected silicon purification, doping, and wafer processing.
  • Silicon cells are stable for 25+ years outdoors with negligible degradation.

Its main weakness is being an indirect-band-gap semiconductor, which makes it a poor light absorber per unit thickness. That is why silicon cells need to be ~100–200 µm thick — a thousand times thicker than direct-gap materials like GaAs or CdTe would require.

title: The p-n Junction Solar Cell
description: How doped silicon turns light into a current

concepts.title: Doping: n-type and p-type
concepts.contentHtml:
Pure silicon barely conducts. To make a working solar cell, two thin layers are doped with impurity atoms:

  • n-type region — doped with phosphorus (5 valence electrons). The extra electron is loosely bound and acts as a free negative charge carrier.
  • p-type region — doped with boron (3 valence electrons). The missing electron — a 'hole' — behaves as a free positive charge carrier.

Concentrations are tiny: about one dopant atom per 10⁶–10⁸ silicon atoms is enough to control conductivity completely. This is the same physics underlying every transistor — solar cells and microelectronics share the same parent technology.

concepts.title: The Depletion Region and Built-in Field
concepts.contentHtml:
Where n-type and p-type silicon meet, electrons diffuse into the p-side and holes diffuse into the n-side. They recombine near the interface, leaving behind exposed dopant ions: positive on the n-side, negative on the p-side. This forms a depletion region — empty of mobile carriers — with a strong built-in electric field pointing from n to p, typically ~10⁵ V/cm across a region only ~1 µm wide.

This field is the engine of the cell. When a photon creates an electron-hole pair anywhere within (or near) the depletion region:

  • The electron is swept into the n-side.
  • The hole is swept into the p-side.

The two charges are now separated. Connecting an external load with wires lets the electron travel through it back to the p-side to recombine — and along the way, it does electrical work.

concepts.title: Cell Architecture in Practice
concepts.contentHtml:
A modern crystalline-silicon cell is layered like this:

  • Anti-reflective coating (often Si₃N₄ — the dark blue colour you see) — reduces reflection from ~30 % bare-silicon down to ~2 %.
  • Front metal grid — fine silver fingers that collect electrons while shading as little of the surface as possible.
  • n-type emitter — thin (~0.5 µm) phosphorus-doped layer at the surface.
  • p-type base — bulk of the wafer (~150 µm), boron-doped.
  • Back surface field & rear contact — heavily doped layer plus aluminium back contact.

A single silicon cell produces about 0.6 V open-circuit and ~10 A in full sun. Cells are wired in series in a module to add voltage, and modules in series and parallel to build a system at useful voltages.

title: Real-World Efficiency
description: I-V curves, fill factor, and where the energy actually goes

concepts.title: The I-V Curve
concepts.contentHtml:
A solar cell's behaviour is summarised by its current-voltage (I-V) curve under standard illumination (1000 W/m², 25 °C, AM1.5 spectrum). Three key points define performance:

  • Short-circuit current I_sc — the current when V = 0 (terminals shorted). Set by how many photons the cell absorbs and converts to carriers.
  • Open-circuit voltage V_oc — the voltage when I = 0 (terminals disconnected). Limited by the band gap and recombination losses; ~0.6–0.7 V for silicon.
  • Maximum power point (V_mp, I_mp) — the operating point that maximises P = IV. Real systems use maximum power point tracking (MPPT) to stay there as light and temperature change.

concepts.title: Where the Energy Goes
concepts.contentHtml:
For a silicon cell illuminated by the standard AM1.5 spectrum (1000 W/m²), the loss budget is roughly:

  • ~19 % — sub-band-gap photons (infrared) pass straight through.
  • ~33 % — above-band-gap excess energy lost as heat (thermalisation).
  • ~16 % — recombination of electron-hole pairs, especially Shockley-Read-Hall and Auger.
  • ~5 % — reflection, shading by metal contacts, ohmic series resistance.
  • ~27 % — useful electricity at the terminals (a top commercial cell delivers 22–24 %).

The two largest losses — sub-bandgap and thermalisation — together waste about half the incident sunlight. They are intrinsic to a single-band-gap material and cannot be eliminated within that constraint.

concepts.title: Temperature and Real-World Performance
concepts.contentHtml:
Solar cells are tested at 25 °C, but in summer a roof module easily reaches 60–70 °C. Performance degrades with temperature for two reasons:

  • The band gap shrinks slightly as temperature rises, lowering V_oc.
  • Reverse saturation current grows, increasing recombination.

For silicon, the temperature coefficient is roughly −0.3 to −0.5 % per °C for power. A panel rated 400 W at 25 °C may deliver only ~340 W at 70 °C.

That is why hot, sunny climates are not always the most productive. Cool, sunny climates — high-altitude desert, or sunny winter days — can outperform tropical roofs on a per-watt basis. Mounting design, ventilation, and tilt all influence module operating temperature.

title: The Shockley-Queisser Limit
description: The theoretical ceiling for a single-junction solar cell

concepts.title: The 1961 Calculation
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1961, William Shockley and Hans Queisser asked: ignoring engineering imperfections entirely, what is the maximum efficiency a single-band-gap solar cell could ever achieve under sunlight?

Their detailed-balance argument used only:

  • The full solar spectrum at the top of Earth's atmosphere (initially treated as a 6000 K black-body).
  • The principle that an excited cell must re-emit thermal radiation in equilibrium.
  • One adjustable parameter — the band gap.

The answer: a maximum efficiency of about 30 % at a band gap near 1.1 eV (close to silicon). With the modern AM1.5G terrestrial spectrum, the optimum shifts slightly upward to a band gap of about 1.34 eV with a maximum efficiency of 33.7 %.

concepts.title: Why a Limit Exists
concepts.contentHtml:
Two losses dominate even the most ideal single-junction cell:

  • Sub-band-gap loss: Photons with energy < E_g are not absorbed at all. Lowering E_g captures more of the spectrum.
  • Thermalisation loss: Photons with energy > E_g create high-energy carriers that quickly drop to the band edge, dumping the excess as heat. Raising E_g reduces this waste.

These two effects pull in opposite directions. The Shockley-Queisser optimum is a balance: low enough to absorb most of the spectrum, high enough to keep the voltage useful. There is also an unavoidable radiative recombination floor — any material that absorbs light must also emit it.

The S-Q limit is not a statement about engineering; it is a statement about thermodynamics. No matter how good your material, antireflective coating, or wiring, a single-band-gap cell cannot exceed ~33.7 % under unconcentrated sunlight.

concepts.title: How Close Are Real Cells?
concepts.contentHtml:
The Shockley-Queisser limit for silicon (E_g = 1.12 eV) is about 32.0 % under AM1.5G. Real records:

  • Lab silicon cell (Kaneka, 2017): 26.7 %
  • Lab GaAs cell (Alta Devices, near-S-Q optimum): 29.1 %
  • Top commercial silicon panel: ~22–24 %

The remaining gap from S-Q is dominated by non-radiative recombination at defects and surfaces. The crystalline-silicon record is now so close to its theoretical limit that further improvements at the cell level are tiny. Future gains have to come from going beyond the single-junction architecture itself.

title: Beyond Shockley-Queisser
description: Multi-junctions, perovskites, and the next generation

concepts.title: Multi-Junction (Tandem) Cells
concepts.contentHtml:
The way around the single-band-gap limit is to use multiple junctions stacked on top of each other, each tuned to a different part of the spectrum:

  • Top cell — wide band gap (e.g. ~1.9 eV) absorbs blue and UV; lets longer wavelengths through.
  • Middle cell — moderate band gap (~1.4 eV) absorbs visible.
  • Bottom cell — narrow band gap (~0.7 eV) absorbs near-infrared.

Thermalisation loss in each layer is greatly reduced because the photons just exceed the local E_g. Theoretical limits rise rapidly:

  • Two-junction tandem: ~42 % under one-sun illumination.
  • Three-junction: ~49 %.
  • Infinite-junction limit: ~68 % under one-sun.

The current world record is 47.6 % (Fraunhofer ISE, 4-junction, concentrated sunlight). Multi-junction cells dominate satellites and concentrator PV but remain too expensive for general rooftop use.

concepts.title: Perovskite-Silicon Tandems
concepts.contentHtml:
Lead-halide perovskites (CH₃NH₃PbI₃ and relatives) appeared in 2009 with single-cell efficiencies of just 3.8 %. By 2024 they had passed 26 % — a faster trajectory than any other PV technology in history. Their band gap is tunable across roughly 1.5–2.3 eV, making them an excellent top-cell partner for silicon.

Perovskite-on-silicon tandems have already exceeded 33 % in the lab, breaking the silicon S-Q ceiling. Commercial products are expected later this decade.

The remaining hurdles are stability (perovskites degrade in heat, moisture, and UV faster than silicon) and the use of lead in the most efficient compositions. Active research targets lead-free analogues and encapsulation strategies to match silicon's 25-year lifetime.

concepts.title: Concentration and Beyond
concepts.contentHtml:
Two further routes raise the practical limit:

  • Concentrator PV (CPV) — focus sunlight onto small high-efficiency cells using lenses or mirrors. Concentration raises V_oc logarithmically and the S-Q limit itself: at 1000-sun concentration the single-junction limit rises to ~40 %, and triple-junction concentrator cells have been demonstrated above 47 %. CPV makes economic sense only in regions with very high direct-normal irradiance.
  • Beyond detailed balance: hot-carrier cells (extract energy before thermalisation), multiple exciton generation (one high-energy photon → two electron-hole pairs in quantum dots), singlet fission (similar effect in organic molecules), and intermediate-band cells. Each promises a route around S-Q in principle; none is yet a commercial product.

The fundamental thermodynamic ceiling under unconcentrated sunlight is the Landsberg limit at about 86 %, requiring an idealised infinite stack of converters. The journey from today's ~24 % to anything close to that is one of the great open challenges in applied physics.
